newsitem.title: UK: North Sea cash Brent feels US inventory pressure.
newsitem.headline: North Sea cash Brent feels US inventory pressure.

text.p: Brent crude slipped further in early paper talk on Wednesday, under pressure from rising stocks in the United States and the prospect of a swift resumption of Iraqi exports under the U.N. oil-for-food deal, traders said.

July Brent shed 13 cents to $18.77 a barrel by 0958 GMT on London's IPE, extending Tuesday's 62-cent slide. Intermonth cash spreads were also weaker, July/August easing to talk at -19/-16 cents after trading at -16 cents twice in late U.S. activity.
"Everything's a bit weaker this morning because of the stocks figures and the fact that the renewal of the Iraqi deal may be faster than expected," said a senior North Sea trader.
American Petroleum Institute (API) figures released late on Tuesday showed U.S. crude stocks jumped by 8.4 million barrels last week despite record gasoline production.
Some analysts cautioned, however, that a large part of the build was in the volatile West Coast region and that the year-on-year surplus fell four million barrels to 14 million barrels.
Benchmark Dated Brent was likely to remain soft under the weight of ample local supply of mid-June cargoes and slack demand in the U.S. Gulf.
CFDs appeared to be easing a cent or two amid talk of the balance of this week trading at July Brent -43 cents.
Only one Brent cargo was expected to be nominated June 19-21 loading dates on Wednesday, traders said.

Other North Sea crudes were starting to slip following Dated Brent's dramatic 60-cent slide of the last 10 days. Early talk was slow but details were emerging of deals on Tuesday which pointed to softer differentials.

A Statfjord cargo due to load June 24-26 was heard trading at Dated Brent +25 cents, three cents weaker than another deal on Tuesday. There was also unconfirmed talk of a Forties deal at +25 cents, some 10 cents weaker than the last reported trade.
